text: The following question stood in the name of  Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar –

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, will Question No 7 be asked again, subsequently?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is a bit of a long answer.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Members have raised three areas of concern with regard to Yale-NUS College's (YNC's) withdrawal of the project originally titled "Dissent and Resistance in Singapore".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The first question they asked was what reasons underpinned the cancellation of the project.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The second was the implications for academic freedom arising from the withdrawal of the project.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And third, what are the rules on what topics and activities are or are not permitted in our autonomous universities (AUs)?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I will lay out the facts of the case, state the Ministry of Education's (MOE's) views on the issue and, finally, set out the principles guiding what activities are permitted or not in all our educational institutions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, the facts of the case and YNC's reasons for withdrawing the project.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The project was to be run by Mr Alfian Sa'at, a playwright.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There have been some media exchanges between YNC and Mr Alfian Sa'at on the details of their correspondences.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Rather than dwell on the details, Mr Speaker, Sir, let me focus on the pertinent facts for the House, which are as follows.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: LAB is a compulsory, credit-bearing programme for all first-year YNC students and they are required to take it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is not an elective or a campus activity.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are clear learning and academic objectives to help students deepen and synergise different subjects they have learnt during the semester, through experiential learning.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second fact, there was no special invitation to Mr Alfian Sa'at.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: He had previously been hired by YNC as a part-time instructor to teach a playwriting course and that was in the first half of 2019.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, when YNC called for project proposals, faculty members and other teaching staff like Mr Alfian Sa'at were invited, and he responded.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Third, from the moment YNC received the outline of his proposal in May 2019, it had questions about how academic objectives were to be achieved.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But the discussions that followed resulted only in a cosmetic title change, from "Dissent and Resistance" to "Dialogue and Dissent".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There were some adjustments to the itinerary, but no substantive change to the overall structure, content or objective of the programme.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Fourth, when YNC received the revised itinerary in September 2019, it became even more concerned.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The proposed project lacked academic rigour and did not expose students to a sufficient range of perspectives.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: From YNC's perspective, if that happened to foreign students, they could lose their student visas.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, to answer Ms Anthea Ong’s question, which was posed to the Minister for Home Affairs as Question No 7, the legal risk was real.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: AUs and their staff and students are not exempt from the law.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: YNC continued to engage Mr Alfian Sa'at to register their concerns and work with him to revise and refine the project itinerary.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: YNC informed MOE of its decision as it expected some public reactions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Fifth, YNC accepts that it could have done better in its administrative processes, in organising the project and communicating their concerns on the project.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But this does not change the basic fact that the proposed project was inappropriately designed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: YNC tried in good faith to work with Mr Alfian Sa'at to make the necessary changes but ran out of time and then decided to withdraw the project.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The report was authored independently from YNC and based on interviews with staff, students, faculty and Mr Alfian Sa'at.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: While a few disagree, most academics, including those from YNC, support the College's decision and its reasons for the decision.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As Assoc Prof Eugene Tan, a law professor from Singapore Management University and former Nominated Member of Parliament told the Straits Times, "For me, the biggest concern is…the lack of even-handedness in engaging with competing and conflicting perspectives… (There is an) absence of even a rudimentary theoretical framework to approach and to understand dissent and resistance." Many members of the public supported YNC's decision, too.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But reading their comments on social media and letters to the newspapers, it is clear their reasons differ from those of academics.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Their concerns were simpler and more fundamental: they did not see why inciting and teaching students to protest should be condoned in our educational institutions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is a valid view that we cannot ignore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: One of those who made this point was Mr Goh Choon Kang, in an opinion piece published in Lianhe Zaobao, which The Straits Times later translated and published, too.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: He worried that there were people seeking to initiate "colour revolutions" in Singapore, that is, revolutions which aim to overthrow governments.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In particular, he was concerned that political dissidence had found its way into our institutes of higher learning (IHLs) and asked if foreigners who backed colour revolutions were trying to extend their influence in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Zaobao and Straits Times published several letters from readers sharing Mr Goh's concern.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I know that these views make some academics and leaders within our AUs a little uncomfortable.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think this is not because they disagree with the views, but because they worry that the public and the Government will overreact, which would affect the academic freedom enjoyed by our AUs today.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They also worry that the Government would henceforth disapprove of Liberal Arts education.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The worry that IHLs may be used to conduct partisan political activities to sow dissent against the Government is not unfounded.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MOE had that concern, too, when we saw the itinerary of the "Dissent and Resistance" project.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It also included talks by Ms Kirsten Han and Dr PJ Thum.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Another part of the project would have entailed watching films celebrating foreign dissidents, including Joshua Wong, the young Hong Kong activist, on the topic "Teenager versus Superpower".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for Mr Alfian Sa'at himself, in 1998, he wrote a poem entitled "Singapore You Are Not My Country".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But Mr Alfian Sa'at continues this attitude consistently in his activism.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In 2013, when 21 Malaysians protested illegally at the Merlion Park, he apologised to Malaysians "on behalf of the Singapore Government" when the protestors were arrested by the Police.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: After the 2018 Malaysian General Election, he praised the "new Malaysia", juxtaposed it favourably against Singapore, and dismissed the fear of "chaos in the streets, clashes with riot police, traffic at a standstill." In a post over the weekend, Mr Alfian wrote of "a revival of student activism in Singapore, especially in areas, such as political conscientisation".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The term "political conscientisation" comes from radical leftwing thought.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It means agitation aimed at making people conscious of the oppression in their lives, so that they will take action against these oppressive elements.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I think this is how Mr Alfian saw his project.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I should add that a talk by the Association of Women for Action and Research in Singapore (AWARE) was also listed in the programme.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But AWARE has since clarified with YNC as well as the media that they had not agreed to participate in the programme, though they had received an invitation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These individuals responsible for the programme are entitled to their views and feelings about Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They can write about them, even vent them on social media; in that process, even have a following.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we have to decide whether we allow such forms of political resistance free rein in our educational institutions and even taught as compulsory, credit-bearing programmes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Some may argue that academic freedom grants universities the licence to run such programmes, in the spirit of critically engaging the minds of our undergraduates.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A few may go even further to claim that dissent is good for democracies and, hence, so is teaching students to become dissidents.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I much prefer the test of an ordinary Singaporean exercising his commonsense.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Dr Intan Mokhtar and Assoc Prof Walter Theseira asked about the implications on academic freedom arising from the withdrawal of this project.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Various academics have, indeed, acknowledged this, and Yale University's independent assessment also came to the same conclusion.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MOE values academic freedom, as do our AUs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With academic freedom, our universities can create new knowledge, innovate and contribute to scientific, technological, economic and social progress.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our AUs have always been places where different ideas are explored and debated, and public discourse carried out vigorously and also rigorously.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is why a liberal arts school like YNC will have a place in Singapore's education landscape.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In fact, in all our AUs, there is increasing focus on interdisciplinary learning and development of critical thinking skills in our students.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But thinking critically is quite different from being unthinkingly critical; and any course offered by our AUs must be up to mark.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Otherwise, it does not deserve to be part of a liberal arts programme.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Political dissent is certainly a legitimate topic of academic inquiry.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our students read and assess classic works by revolutionary figures, such as Marx, Engels, Lenin, Sun Yat Sen or Mao Zedong.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It would also be valuable for students in the social sciences to examine critically present-day issues, such as the causes and implications of protests against climate change or globalisation, or the demonstrations currently happening in Hong Kong.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Students can and should also discuss the implications of such political developments on a small country like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It would not be practical or wise to be overly prescriptive in specifying what should or should not be taught in each subject.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have to leave room for the AUs to exercise their good judgement.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our laws are enacted by Parliament, which comprises Members of Parliament who are, in turn, elected by voters.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These laws are the democratic expression of the will of the people.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our educational institutions must operate and exercise their academic freedom, within those legal limits.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is a principle that the founding President of YNC and the current Vice-President of Yale University, Prof Pericles Lewis, publicly committed to in 2012.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Clarifying YNC's policy regarding freedom of expression, he said "any college or university must obey the laws of the countries where it operates".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Every country has their rules and laws, red lines unique to themselves.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, I do not think the US would tolerate an American university course designed by Jihadists to promote violence, or that France or Germany would accept a course teaching that Nazism is good.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Exploring and debating issues within the context of academic study helps students develop important critical thinking skills.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This should be underpinned by rigorous intellectual reasoning, with students required to understand and interpret events and facts within a coherent intellectual framework and, at the same time, to examine theories against the facts and empirical evidence, and against competing theories or arguments.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is especially important when studying complex and potentially controversial issues.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Prof Rajeev Patke, Director of YNC’s humanities division, put it very well.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In an email to the College leadership, he wrote, "To study is distinct from to practise: to study 'contemporary resistance' or 'contemporary violence' or 'contemporary prejudice' is not the same as to practise resistance, violence or prejudice.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have to ensure that in our educational institutions, academic study does not get confused or compromised by courses of action and intervention which belong to the realm of individual choice." In Singapore's democracy, there are many avenues for political parties and activists to champion their causes, and for people to make their choices and exercise their political rights.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Educational institutions, and especially the formal curriculum, are not the platforms to do this.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When elections are impending, AUs will always host panel discussions comprising representatives from various political parties and seek to present a balanced range of viewpoints.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Otherwise, politicians of any political party – Government or Opposition – may not campaign, mobilise support or advance their party politics in any of our educational institutions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This has always been the position – always been.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When political officeholders attend events, give speeches or conduct dialogues with students, they will do so only for the purpose of discussing national policies, not to mobilise partisan political support.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Every society is a product of its history, culture and unique circumstances, which set the context of what is acceptable and how things are done.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our governance approach is shaped by our unique realities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are a small, multiracial and multi-religious country.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our margin for error is very small compared to bigger countries.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Imagine if the demonstrations and riots on the streets of Hong Kong, or the political confusion in the UK, were to take place in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Trust and confidence in Singapore, whether by Singaporeans or others, would be severely damaged.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Singapore has been able to progress and develop, not least because we have maintained stability.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have built strong governing institutions, engendered respect for the rule of law and engaged deeply with citizens.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have found solutions and struck compromises before the problems become so severe.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We did not wait for protests and strikes to break out before solving the problems downstream.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But instead, the Government, employers and unions forged a compact amongst themselves, resolved problems and disputes upstream, and thus maintained industrial harmony.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This also made Singapore an attractive investment destination.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We adopt the same approach in tackling many other challenges, be it housing, ageing population or climate change.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Recognise the challenges early, take a long-term view, find solutions, discuss, find compromises and prevent problems from spiralling beyond control.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We should strengthen this collective, constructive approach and avoid falling into the divisions and dissensions that plague other societies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is a fact of life that good things always get carried to excesses and then get misused.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Free market competition is a good thing, and so is capitalism; they promise more jobs and better lives for people, but they are often marred by greed and exploitation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Democracy remains the best system of governance known to humankind, but faith in the system can be weakened by populism and divisive politics.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Social media connect people and give voice to the previously voiceless, but falsehoods and manipulation can also proliferate in that space, too.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In all these instances, society needs to recognise the problem and respond, and governments need to intervene in order to preserve the positive objectives and merits of the systems, what they set out to do.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Modern-day Galileos would not exist without our academics and researchers being free to pursue the truth, understand nature, wherever it may lead.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But let us also be aware that given the state of the world today, there will be people who want to misuse it as a cloak to advance their hidden agendas, sometimes not even very hidden.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To preserve what we cherish, we must be ready to protect it when the situation calls for it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Academic institutions should internalise the principles I stated earlier.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Governance everywhere, of countries, companies and educational institutions, has become far more complex because of technology and the free flow of information.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Governance calls for judgement and that judgement has to reflect the country's norms.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Most countries share fundamental values, such as the rule of law, incorruptibility and open discourse.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But the way these values are expressed will vary from country to country, depending on their histories, social values and cultures.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In some societies, individuals are more concerned about how far can I extend my fist.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But in Singapore, Singaporeans worry when my fist will reach your nose.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We must certainly work across boundaries and learn from one another, but we must do so while understanding and respecting one another’s contexts and norms.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is the best strategy for Singapore to progress and live peacefully in a diverse and interconnected world.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One is, with this incident, what does it mean for the future of YNC?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Ministry sort of exercise greater scrutiny on YNC over the programmes it carries out or the lecturers or academics that it engages?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And two, can we still continue to have a liberal arts education here in Singapore, bearing in mind our local context?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I will answer the second question first and then the first.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, from that perspective, we value the partnership with Yale in running YNC because they bring us a good quality liberal arts education.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: From Yale University's perspective, they value that partnership, too, because they can then have a liberal arts education delivered in Asia in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In fact, I would like to add that in the National University of Singapore (NUS), there is a University Scholars Programme, which is quite similar to a liberal arts education.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For the partnership between Yale and NUS to work, both sides must agree to abide by the principles I set out earlier.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The standard of the project is so far off the mark, I think both sides agree there are no implications on academic freedom.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But I would not rule out that, in time to come, there will be incidents that test our partnership.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When that happens, I expect both sides to have to constantly evaluate the strength of our understanding and adherence to the principles I stated earlier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The first is, would the Minister agree that the AUs should develop clear guidelines for assessing academic rigour and to communicate that clearly to faculty and external parties?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The governance concern here is that these standards were not communicated early and properly to the relevant parties, and that makes the decision seem arbitrary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The second question is that the Minister expressed concerns about the suitability of numerous individuals connected to the case and he outlined the criteria for what makes a suitable educator or facilitator.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I wish to ask if this means that the policy is that there should be a blacklist of sorts, that our AUs should not engage individuals on this kind of list that would meet these criteria.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I think this is concerning, because it raises the risk that the universities will overreact and put people on such a list when they should not be.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The first point is a fair one and I would expect AUs to have clear guidelines on how they set their academic standards.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If it is not done robustly or detailed enough or not communicated well enough, I would encourage them to do so.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for the second issue, I think we have to leave a lot of room for educational institutions to decide for themselves.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Whether a person is suitable to be a teacher or instructor at all, that is a relevant consideration.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because, in universities, to be a tenured professor, it is a very high bar.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have to leave room for the universities to exercise judgement.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Is a person who is an activist, therefore, not suitable to teach?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The world over, academics and faculty are encouraged to be activists because you cannot just focus on publications and citations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To realise the impact of research and your work, faculty are encouraged to be active.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, translate your findings into patents, enterprises or, if it is in the social sciences, discuss with the Ministries your ideas and see if you can contribute to policymaking.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, activism amongst faculty is actually quite encouraged.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The second question then is: how about political activism?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You cannot conflate them within a classroom; you have to keep them separate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And so long as they are kept separate, there is actually no problem.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In fact, we have Members of Parliament, both People's Action Party Members of Parliament as well as Opposition Members of Parliament, who are faculty members.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And so long as they can keep those two activities separate, it is not a problem at all.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But, of course, there is a third aspect, which is, what political activism does the person stand for?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Remember, in many American universities, if someone, if a faculty is sexist or racist, he will not be engaged, no matter how good his research or teaching is.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If you are convicted of a sexual offence, even if you are an Oscar Academy Award winner, the studios will not engage you.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Therefore, it is not just the content of the course but also what the instructor stands for.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, depending on the person's history and track record, educational institutions, I am sure, will consider carefully whether this is someone they want to engage at all.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier in his answer, he mentioned that for this particular incident when the project was pulled, Yale had its own independent report after it reviewed the incident.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, the Minister also articulated the Ministry's position on the matter.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, I just need to clarify whether the review of this particular project was initiated by the Ministry or was it YNC's own introspection that led them to review the matter.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The simple answer is that it was their own introspection and then they informed us after that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And, of course, as they expected, Yale University then raised an eyebrow, they wanted to find out what happened and so they did an independent report by Yale University's Vice President, Prof Pericles Lewis, and they confirmed and they are satisfied that this withdrawal does not affect academic freedom in the university.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The first is on the four principles which the Minister had outlined.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Assuming all the AUs come up with their own guidelines on what would guide them in terms of the curriculum, in the event these principles and their guidelines are not complied with, how will the Ministry intervene, if at all, and what form of intervention could this take?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: My second supplementary question – and this is something I have raised previously – is that in the area of certain topics, whether it is political science or liberal arts, I think a good sensing of the local context is very important.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is where my bias is towards having more local academics than ones who are foreign-based, whether we need to achieve some form of or calibrate the right balance.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, my question to the Minister is whether something more deliberate and comprehensive could be put in place to address that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If it is breached, whether there will be an intervention from the Ministry, all I can say is that I stand before this House to answer on behalf of AU issues about sexual misconduct in campus, about how their endowment funds are raised and used, and recently about international students in AUs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I, as well as my colleagues in MOE, we are accountable to the House about what happens in the AUs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, should something go wrong, it is our duty and responsibility to also work with the university to resolve the problems and be accountable to the House.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Having said that, I would not characterise the relationship between MOE and the universities as a regulator-regulatee kind of relationship.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They express their concerns to us and likewise, and we find compromises, consensus on how to move forward.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And that is the kind of relationship we want.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Just last week, we had a workplan seminar.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But apart from that, on the issue of context and understanding Singapore's context and teaching and doing research within Singapore's context, I would say that it is not just for locals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A foreign faculty can also acquire that sensitivity to our context.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I would say it is not so much on that front.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is not so much a local versus foreign issue but that I think all academics and our institutions will have to understand Singapore's context and operate within it.
